matching.reasoningTemplate: Cytopenias with bleeding, infections and blasts on film suggest acute leukaemia.

harrison.pages: 825-834 (AML, Ch.109), 844-848 (ALL, Ch.111), 591-593 (oncologic emergencies: leukostasis, tumor lysis syndrome), 575 (febrile neutropenia)
clinicalPearls: AML accounts for ~31% of new acute leukaemias but ~62% of leukaemic deaths; it is the commonest acute leukaemia in older adults (median age ~69), whereas ALL peaks in young children (age 3-4) and again in the elderly (Harrison 22e p.825, p.844).

Presentation is usually nonspecific and reflects marrow failure: fatigue (often the first symptom), anorexia/weight loss, bleeding/easy bruising, and fever; about half of AML patients have symptoms for 3 months or less before diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.828).
Auer rods (rod-shaped cytoplasmic granules) on the blood film establish a myeloid lineage with certainty and are not seen in ALL (Harrison 22e p.828).
Gum (gingival) hypertrophy and skin/soft-tissue infiltration are characteristic of monocytic AML subtypes and KMT2A-rearranged disease (Harrison 22e p.828).

A myeloid sarcoma (chloroma) is a tissue mass of myeloid blasts (skin, lymph node, GI tract, soft tissue, testis); isolated myeloid sarcoma rapidly progresses to marrow/blood involvement and cannot be cured by local therapy alone (Harrison 22e p.828).

Median presenting WBC in AML is ~15,000/uL; 20% present with >100,000/uL and <5% have no circulating blasts. In ALL ~40% have normal or low WBC and 8% have no circulating blasts, so an automated count can miss the diagnosis - always review the smear (Harrison 22e p.828, p.844).

Diagnosis requires examination of blood AND bone marrow; biopsy distinguishes AML from ALL, and cytochemistry, flow-cytometric immunophenotyping, cytogenetics and molecular studies are all needed for subtyping (Harrison 22e p.828, p.844).

Diagnosis no longer rests on the historical >=20% blast threshold alone - the 2022 WHO classification removed the blast-percent requirement for AML defined by specific genetic lesions such as t(15;17), t(8;21), inv(16) and NPM1 mutation (Harrison 22e p.826).

DIC and coagulopathy are classically associated with acute promyelocytic leukaemia (t(15;17)/PML-RARA); APL bleeding can be catastrophic (GI, intrapulmonary, intracranial), and paradoxically thrombosis can also occur (Harrison 22e p.828).

CSF examination is routine in ALL: CNS leukaemia is defined by >=5 cells/uL or blasts on morphology; CNS involvement is present at diagnosis in 5-10% of adults (higher in mature B-ALL and T-ALL). Defer/limit lumbar puncture if platelets <20 x10^9/L or active bleeding (Harrison 22e p.844-845).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute leukaemia is a clonal proliferation of immature, poorly differentiated haematopoietic precursors (blasts) that infiltrate marrow, blood and other tissues; AML arises from myeloid progenitors and ALL from lymphoid (B- or T-lineage) progenitors. Genome sequencing indicates most AML arises from a small number of mutations that accumulate with age - up to 5-6% of normal people over 70 carry premalignant clones (clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, CHIP, commonly DNMT3A/TET2/ASXL1), which carries a ~10-fold increased risk of haematologic malignancy though additional 'hits' are required to progress to overt leukaemia. Genetic lesions drive both phenotype and behaviour: for example t(15;17)/PML-RARA defines APL and predisposes to DIC, while NPM1 and FLT3 mutations associate with high leukocyte counts. Marrow replacement by blasts produces anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, accounting for the dominant clinical features (Harrison 22e p.825-828, p.844).
additionalDifferentials: Acute myeloid leukaemia vs acute lymphoblastic leukaemia - distinguished by morphology (Auer rods imply AML), cytochemistry, flow-cytometric immunophenotype and genetics (Harrison 22e p.828, p.844)
Myelodysplastic syndrome or myeloproliferative neoplasm evolving to acute leukaemia (antecedent haematologic disorder) (Harrison 22e p.828)
Therapy-related (secondary) acute leukaemia after alkylating agents (4-6 yr) or topoisomerase II inhibitors (1-3 yr) (Harrison 22e p.826)
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood smear (Wright-Giemsa) with manual differential - essential at presentation; look for blasts and Auer rods (Harrison 22e p.828, p.844)
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for morphology, cytochemistry, flow-cytometric immunophenotyping, cytogenetics and molecular studies (Harrison 22e p.829, p.844)
Cytogenetics/karyotype and molecular panel at diagnosis (NPM1, FLT3-ITD/TKD, CEBPA, TP53, IDH1/IDH2, RUNX1 etc.) - the most important prognostic data in AML (Harrison 22e p.827-828)
Serum uric acid, electrolytes including potassium, phosphate and calcium, creatinine/BUN, and LDH to assess and monitor tumour-lysis risk (Harrison 22e p.829, p.593)
Coagulation panel - PT, aPTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer - to detect DIC, especially when APL is suspected (Harrison 22e p.829)
Measurable (minimal) residual disease assessment by multiparameter flow cytometry or molecular methods (e.g. PCR for PML-RARA in APL) for response monitoring (Harrison 22e p.827, p.834, p.847)
Lumbar puncture/CSF cytology in ALL (and AML with neurologic symptoms) to detect CNS involvement (Harrison 22e p.845)
Urinalysis for uric acid crystals; urinary uric acid:creatinine ratio >1 supports acute uric-acid nephropathy (Harrison 22e p.593)
redFlags: Suspected APL (ecchymoses/oozing from IV sites, DIC) - a haematologic emergency; coagulopathy can be rapidly fatal and warrants prompt differentiation therapy (Harrison 22e p.828, p.834)

Hyperleukocytosis with blast count >100,000/uL and leukostasis - brain (stupor, headache, visual change, confusion, coma, sudden death) or lung (dyspnoea, hypoxaemia, respiratory failure); a potentially fatal emergency, especially in AML (Harrison 22e p.591)
Tumour lysis syndrome - hyperkalaemia (risk of fatal arrhythmia), hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia (tetany), hyperuricaemia and acute kidney injury (Harrison 22e p.592-593)
Febrile neutropenia (fever with granulocytes <1500/uL) - medical emergency requiring urgent empirical antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.575)
CNS symptoms - headache, visual change, focal/non-focal neurologic deficit - may indicate CNS leukaemia or intracranial bleed (Harrison 22e p.829-830)
harrison.prognosis: Outcome is dominated by age and genetics. In AML, cytogenetic/molecular findings at diagnosis are the strongest predictors: t(15;17)/APL has a very good prognosis (~85% cured), core-binding-factor AML (t(8;21), inv(16)) is favourable (~55% cured), normal-karyotype AML is intermediate (~40% cured), and TP53 mutation, complex karyotype, t(6;9), inv(3) or monosomy 7 are adverse with little chance of cure without transplant. NPM1 mutation without FLT3-ITD is favourable, whereas FLT3-ITD is adverse. Advancing age, poor performance status, antecedent haematologic disorder/preceding cytopenias, therapy-related disease and high presenting WBC all worsen outcome; only ~32% of AML patients survive 5 years overall. In ALL, outcome is strongly age-dependent - cure rates ~90% in children falling to <10% in elderly/frail adults; achievement of molecular complete remission (MRD negativity) is the most important on-treatment prognostic factor (Harrison 22e p.825-828, p.846-847).
pitfalls: Relying on an automated blood count can miss acute leukaemia - 8% of ALL patients (and <5% of AML) have no circulating blasts; review the smear (Harrison 22e p.828, p.844).

In hyperleukocytosis, arterial blood gas oxygen tension can be spuriously low because the high WBC mass consumes plasma oxygen in the sample; use pulse oximetry to assess oxygenation (Harrison 22e p.591).
High leukocyte and platelet counts can cause pseudohyperkalaemia from cell lysis after the blood is drawn (no ECG changes) - follow plasma rather than serum potassium (Harrison 22e p.593).
Avoid unnecessary RBC transfusion and intravascular volume depletion in hyperleukocytosis - both raise blood viscosity and can worsen leukostasis (Harrison 22e p.591).
Urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate is no longer recommended for tumour-lysis prophylaxis (Harrison 22e p.593).

Even minor bleeding in a thrombocytopenic leukaemia patient justifies immediate platelet transfusion because qualitative platelet dysfunction and infection increase bleeding risk independent of the count (Harrison 22e p.829).
harrison.severityClassification: AML is classified by the WHO 2022 system primarily on defining genetic abnormalities (e.g. PML-RARA, RUNX1-RUNX1T1, CBFB-MYH11, KMT2A rearrangement, NPM1 or CEBPA mutation) and, where genetics are absent, by differentiation; the historical >=20%-blast diagnostic threshold has been removed for genetically defined entities. Prognostic risk is stratified by the 2022 European LeukemiaNet (ELN) scheme into favourable, intermediate and adverse categories based on cytogenetic and molecular findings at diagnosis (APL is risk-stratified separately, low- vs high-risk by presenting WBC, threshold 10,000/uL). ALL is subtyped immunologically into B-lineage and T-lineage, with risk stratification (standard vs high) using age, WBC count, immunophenotype, cytogenetics/molecular lesions (notably Ph/BCR-ABL) and MRD status (Harrison 22e p.826-827, p.834, p.846-847).
